questions.stem: A student tests how the concentration of salt in water affects the germination rate of wheat seeds. The dependent variable is:
options: the type of wheat seed used
the temperature of the incubator
the germination rate of the seeds
the concentration of salt in the water
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change, here the germination rate. Salt concentration is the independent variable, which the student deliberately changes.

questions.stem: In the salt and germination experiment, which is a controlled variable?
options: The percentage of seeds that germinate
The volume of solution added to each dish
The concentration of salt added to each dish
The number of seeds that germinate
questions.explanation: Controlled variables are kept the same so that only the independent variable affects the result. Salt concentration is the independent variable, and germination counts or percentages are the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Which is the best hypothesis for an investigation into whether leaf litter depth affects the number of invertebrates in a forest?
options: Invertebrates are important decomposers that live in the leaf litter of most forests
If leaf litter depth increases, then the number of invertebrates per quadrat will increase
Leaf litter depth may or may not have some effect on invertebrates living on the forest floor
The aim is to find out what happens to invertebrates in deep and shallow leaf litter
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that links the independent and dependent variables. A statement that something may or may not happen cannot be tested, and an aim or background fact is not a hypothesis.

questions.stem: A student compares algal growth in pond water with and without added fertiliser. Why should she also set up flasks of pond water with no fertiliser, under identical conditions?
options: They act as a control, showing what growth occurs without the independent variable
They increase the number of independent variables, making the experiment more valid
They remove the need to repeat the experiment, because they confirm the result
They allow the fertiliser concentration to be calculated from the algal growth
questions.explanation: A control group shows the baseline result without the treatment, so any difference can be attributed to the fertiliser. Testing more than one independent variable at once would reduce validity, not improve it.

questions.stem: To test whether shade affects soil temperature, a student measures soil under a tree in the morning and soil in an open paddock in the afternoon. What is the main problem with this design?
options: Shade is a dependent variable, so it should be measured rather than changed
Time of day is not controlled, so the effect of shade cannot be separated from it
Soil temperature is a qualitative variable, so it cannot be measured with a thermometer
The sample size is too large, which makes the data less precise than a single reading
questions.explanation: Soil temperature changes over the day, so measuring the two sites at different times mixes the effect of time with the effect of shade. Both sites should be measured at the same time, ideally with repeats.

questions.stem: Which investigation methodology involves collating and analysing secondary data from other people's scientific findings?
options: Fieldwork
Simulation
Literature review
Controlled experiment
questions.explanation: A literature review collates and analyses secondary data and viewpoints from published sources. Fieldwork and controlled experiments generate primary data from the student's own observations or measurements.

questions.stem: A student records the number of frog calls and the water temperature at 20 wetlands without changing any conditions. Which methodology is this?
options: Controlled experiment
Literature review
Product development
Correlational study
questions.explanation: Planned observation of variables that are not manipulated, to find associations between them, is a correlational study. No variable is deliberately changed, so it is not a controlled experiment.

questions.stem: Students use a computer model to explore how a catchment's stream flow would respond to different rainfall scenarios over 50 years. This methodology is:
options: fieldwork
classification
simulation
case study
questions.explanation: A simulation uses a model to study a system whose variables are too complex, slow or large to manipulate directly. A 50-year catchment response could not be tested by fieldwork within a school year.

questions.stem: Fieldwork finds that sites with more fox scats have fewer bandicoots. Why can the student not conclude from this alone that foxes cause the decline?
options: Fieldwork shows a correlation, and another factor such as habitat quality could affect both
Fieldwork can only produce qualitative data, so no relationship can be found at all
Fieldwork always establishes causation, so the conclusion needs no further testing
Fieldwork data are secondary, so they cannot be used to draw any conclusions
questions.explanation: Fieldwork usually identifies correlation rather than a causal relationship. A third variable, such as vegetation cover, might favour foxes and disadvantage bandicoots at the same time. Fieldwork can generate quantitative primary data.

questions.stem: Which sampling technique is most suitable for estimating the population size of a mobile animal such as a skink?
options: Line transect
Square quadrat
Belt transect
Mark-recapture
questions.explanation: Mark-recapture is designed for mobile animals that cannot all be counted at once. Quadrats and transects suit plants and slow-moving organisms that stay in place while being counted.

questions.stem: Why should quadrats be placed using random coordinates on a grid rather than where the student chooses?
options: To make sure every quadrat contains the same number of plant species
To reduce the number of quadrats that need to be sampled overall
To make sure every quadrat falls on the edge of the habitat
To avoid bias towards areas that look interesting or easy to sample
questions.explanation: Random placement gives every part of the site an equal chance of being sampled, avoiding observer bias. It does not make quadrats contain equal numbers of species, which would defeat the purpose of sampling.

questions.stem: How does increasing the number of quadrats sampled in a woodland affect the data?
options: The estimate is less likely to represent the woodland, because more quadrats add more errors
The estimate becomes exact, because every species is certain to be recorded once enough quadrats are used
The estimate is unaffected in reliability, because only the quadrat size controls reliability
The estimate is more likely to represent the whole woodland, as chance variation has less influence
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce the influence of chance variation, so the data are more robust and representative. More samples improve the estimate but cannot make it exact, because a sample is never the whole population.

questions.stem: A student samples five 1 m² quadrats in a large paddock and records 3 species. A second student samples 30 quadrats and records 11 species. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The smaller sample was more accurate because it disturbed less of the site
The paddock changed so quickly that the samples must have been taken years apart
The small sample missed less common species that the larger sample detected
The larger sample created new species by disturbing more of the paddock
questions.explanation: Rare species are often missed by small samples, so species richness tends to rise with sampling effort until it levels off. A plot of species found against quadrats sampled helps decide when the sample is large enough.

questions.stem: In VCE Environmental Science, accuracy describes how:
options: well a measurement matches the result the student predicted
close a measurement is to the true value of the quantity
closely a set of repeated measurements agree with each other
many decimal places a measuring instrument is able to display
questions.explanation: A measurement is accurate if it is close to the true value. How closely repeated measurements agree with each other is precision, which says nothing about closeness to the true value.

questions.stem: A measurement is said to be valid if it:
options: has been recorded to many significant figures
measures what it is supposed to be measuring
gives the same value every time it is repeated
is close to the value found by other scientists
questions.explanation: Validity is about whether the measurement or experiment investigates what it claims to. A measurement can be repeatable without being valid, for example if the wrong quantity is measured consistently.

questions.stem: Five readings of pH in a lake are 6.1, 6.2, 6.1, 6.2 and 6.1, but a calibrated reference meter shows the true pH is 7.0. The readings are:
options: both accurate and precise
neither accurate nor precise
precise but not accurate
accurate but not precise
questions.explanation: The readings agree closely with each other, so they are precise. They are all about 0.9 below the true value, so they are not accurate, which suggests a systematic error such as a poorly calibrated meter.

questions.stem: A student measures stream turbidity five times in an hour with the same meter and method, and gets closely matching results. This shows good:
options: reproducibility
accuracy
validity
repeatability
questions.explanation: Repeatability is agreement between successive measurements under the same conditions: same method, observer, instrument and location over a short time. Reproducibility refers to agreement under changed conditions, such as a different observer or instrument.

questions.stem: A university team measures phosphate in the same creek using a different method and instruments, and obtains results close to a school class's. What does this show about the class's results?
options: They are repeatable, because the same method was used twice
They are now known to be exactly equal to the true value
They are invalid, because two different methods were used
They are reproducible, which increases confidence in them
questions.explanation: Agreement under changed conditions, such as a different method, observer and instrument, is reproducibility. Repeatability requires the same conditions. Agreement increases confidence but cannot prove the results equal the true value.

questions.stem: A student wants to know how road runoff affects water quality in a creek, but measures only water temperature. What is the main weakness of this investigation?
options: Its accuracy is low, because thermometers always read higher than the true temperature
Its validity is low, because temperature alone does not measure the pollutants in road runoff
Its precision is low, because temperature can only be measured to the nearest whole degree Celsius
Its repeatability is low, because water temperature can never be measured more than once
questions.explanation: Road runoff mainly carries pollutants such as sediment, oils and metals, so temperature alone does not measure what the student set out to investigate. The data could be precise and repeatable and still not answer the question.

questions.stem: A data logger's temperature probe reads 0.5 °C too high every time. This is an example of:
options: a random error
a personal error
an outlier
a systematic error
questions.explanation: A systematic error shifts every reading in the same direction by a consistent amount, affecting accuracy. Random errors cause unpredictable scatter in both directions.

questions.stem: Which is the most effective way to reduce the effect of random errors on a measured value?
options: Take more repeated measurements and calculate a mean
Recalibrate the instrument against a known standard
Change the independent variable by larger amounts
Discard any reading that differs from the prediction
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter readings both above and below the true value, so averaging many readings reduces their effect. Recalibration corrects a systematic error, and discarding unexpected readings introduces bias.

questions.stem: Why does repeating measurements not improve accuracy when a systematic error is present?
options: Systematic errors only affect the first reading, so repeats are unaffected
Repeats remove precision, so the mean becomes further from the true value
Every reading is shifted by the same amount, so the mean is shifted too
Repeated readings increase the systematic error each time they are taken
questions.explanation: A systematic error moves all readings in one direction, so averaging them leaves the same offset. It must be found and removed, for example by calibration. Repeats do help reduce random error.

questions.stem: A student misreads a measuring cylinder by looking at it from above, and records one value incorrectly. In VCE Environmental Science this is classed as:
options: a random error, which should be reduced by averaging it with the other readings taken
a systematic error, which should be corrected by recalibrating the cylinder
an uncertainty, which should be reported as the range of the true value
a personal error, which should be eliminated by repeating the measurement correctly
questions.explanation: Mistakes and observer errors such as parallax are personal errors. They are not part of the analysis of data quality; the measurement should simply be done again correctly.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes error from uncertainty?
options: Error and uncertainty are the same idea, both describing a mistake made by the person taking the measurement
Error applies only to counting measurements; uncertainty applies only to readings taken with an electronic instrument
Error is the difference between a measured and true value; uncertainty is the range in which the true value is expected to lie
Error is the range in which the true value is expected to lie; uncertainty is the difference between a measured and true value
questions.explanation: The study design defines error as the difference between the measured and true values and uncertainty as the range within which the true value is expected to lie. They are not synonyms, and neither refers to a personal mistake.

questions.stem: Five readings of dissolved oxygen are 8.1, 8.3, 8.2, 3.9 and 8.2 mg/L. What should the student do with the 3.9 mg/L reading?
options: Replace it with 8.2 mg/L, because that is the value the student expected to find
Investigate it, for example by repeating the reading and checking the method, before deciding
Delete it at once, because any reading that differs from the others must be a mistake
Include it in the mean without comment, because removing data is always unethical
questions.explanation: Outliers must be further analysed and accounted for rather than automatically dismissed. Repeating the reading may reveal a fault or a real local effect. Replacing data with expected values is falsification.

questions.stem: Which type of graph is most suitable for showing how mean daily water temperature in a river changes over a year?
options: Flow chart
Line graph
Bar chart
Pie chart
questions.explanation: A line graph shows how a continuous variable changes over time and makes trends and cycles visible. A bar chart suits comparisons between separate categories, such as different sites.

questions.stem: A frog survey counted 160 frogs in 2015 and 120 in 2020. What was the percentage change?
options: 75% decrease
25% decrease
33% decrease
40% decrease
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (120 − 160) ÷ 160 × 100 = −25%, a 25% decrease. Dividing by the final value of 120 gives about 33%, a common slip. 75% is the 2020 count as a percentage of 2015.

questions.stem: Four quadrats contain 12, 15, 9 and 14 seedlings. What is the mean number of seedlings per quadrat?
questions.explanation: Mean = (12 + 15 + 9 + 14) ÷ 4 = 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5. The median is 13, which is a different measure, and 50 is the total rather than the mean.

questions.stem: A graph of carbon dioxide concentration from 1960 to 2000 is used to estimate the value in 2030 by continuing the trend line. This process is called:
options: correlation
extrapolation
interpolation
calibration
questions.explanation: Extrapolation estimates values beyond the range of the data, which carries more uncertainty because the trend may change. Interpolation estimates values within the range of measured data.

questions.stem: A graph shows strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and bushfire numbers in a region across the year. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Both are probably linked to a third factor, such as hot weather, rather than one causing the other
Ice cream sales cause bushfires, because the two variables rise and fall at the same time
Bushfires cause ice cream sales, because people buy ice cream when there is smoke
The correlation is meaningless, because correlations never reveal anything about causes
questions.explanation: Correlation does not prove causation; hot, dry weather plausibly drives both. Correlations are still useful for suggesting relationships to test, so they are not meaningless.

questions.stem: A graph of atmospheric carbon dioxide over several years shows a rise and fall within each year on top of a rising trend. This data shows:
options: a cyclical pattern with no long-term change at all
a cyclical pattern superimposed on an increasing trend
a linear pattern with no variation at all from year to year
a decreasing trend with random variation each year
questions.explanation: The repeating yearly rise and fall is a cyclical pattern, and the overall rise is a long-term trend. Identifying both is part of processing data for linear, non-linear and cyclical patterns.

questions.stem: Before using a chemical reagent to test nitrate levels in water, a student should consult which document for its hazards and safe handling?
options: The safety data sheet (SDS)
The student's investigation logbook
The scientific poster
The literature review
questions.explanation: A safety data sheet gives a chemical's hazards, safe handling, storage and first aid, and informs the risk assessment. The logbook records the investigation but is not the source of hazard information.

questions.stem: A risk assessment for fieldwork at a river identifies the risk of slipping into fast-flowing water. Which is the best control measure?
options: Sampling from a stable bank using an extendable sampling pole
Recording the hazard in the logbook and then wading in as planned
Working faster so that less time is spent near the water's edge
Sampling alone so that fewer people are exposed to the hazard
questions.explanation: A good control measure reduces the likelihood or consequence of the hazard, such as removing the need to enter the water. Merely recording a hazard does not control it, and working alone increases the danger.

questions.stem: A student surveys local residents' attitudes to a proposed wind farm. Which action best demonstrates ethical conduct?
options: Telling residents the survey is anonymous while recording their addresses
Obtaining informed consent and keeping respondents' identities confidential
Recording residents' names with their answers so that results can be checked
Including only the responses that support the student's hypothesis
questions.explanation: Ethical research with people requires informed consent, confidentiality and honest reporting. Selecting only supporting responses misrepresents the data, and deceiving participants breaches their trust.

questions.stem: A student plans to measure the effect of a pesticide on native earthworms by exposing them to high concentrations until they die. Which response best reflects ethical guidelines?
options: Proceed, but use as many earthworms as possible so that the results will be more reliable
Use introduced earthworms instead, because ethical guidelines apply only to native species
Refine the design to use the fewest animals and least harm, such as sub-lethal measures or a simulation
Proceed as planned, because invertebrates are not covered by any ethical considerations at all
questions.explanation: Ethical conduct involves minimising harm and the number of animals used, and considering alternatives. More animals than needed is not justified, and ethical care is not limited to native species or to vertebrates.

questions.stem: A student builds a physical model of a catchment from a tray of soil, plastic sheeting and a watering can to study runoff. What is a key limitation of this model?
options: It is more complex than the real catchment, so its results are harder to interpret
It produces only secondary data, so the results cannot be analysed or graphed
It simplifies factors such as soil depth, vegetation and rainfall patterns in a real catchment
It cannot be used to make any predictions, because physical models never represent reality in any way
questions.explanation: Models simplify reality so that a system can be studied, but they leave out or scale down real factors, which limits how far results can be applied. They still allow testable predictions and can generate primary data.

questions.stem: A mathematical model predicts that a koala population will fall by 30% over 20 years. Which step would most increase confidence in the model?
options: Running the model again with the same inputs to see if it gives the same output
Adding more decimal places to the predicted population figures
Publishing the prediction in the media to see if the public agrees
Checking that the model reproduces past population counts when given past conditions
questions.explanation: Testing a model against independent observed data shows whether it represents the real system. Re-running a deterministic model with the same inputs will give the same answer, which tests nothing about its validity.

questions.stem: A farmer says, 'I saw more platypus in the creek after the fence went up, so fencing works.' This is best described as:
options: an anecdote
a controlled experiment
a mathematical model
a reproducible result
questions.explanation: An anecdote is an individual account or observation that has not been systematically collected or tested. It may suggest a hypothesis, but it is weak evidence compared with systematic surveys.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence most strongly supports a claim that a new stormwater wetland has improved water quality?
options: A single water sample taken downstream on one sunny day after construction
Repeated measurements of nutrients upstream and downstream, before and after construction
A council media release stating that the wetland is working as it was designed to
Residents reporting that the creek looks cleaner since the wetland was completed
questions.explanation: Strong evidence comes from systematic, repeated measurements with comparisons that isolate the effect. A single sample, opinions and promotional statements are weak evidence, even if they agree with the claim.

questions.stem: A student's hypothesis was that more shade lowers water temperature. Her data show a weak trend in that direction with large variation and only three samples per site. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The data prove the hypothesis, because the trend is in the predicted direction
The data disprove the hypothesis, because there is variation between samples
No conclusion can ever be drawn from fieldwork, so the investigation should be abandoned
The data provide limited support for the hypothesis; more samples are needed to be confident
questions.explanation: A conclusion should state how far the evidence supports the hypothesis and recommend improvements, such as a larger sample. Data never prove a hypothesis, and variation alone does not disprove it.

questions.stem: Why must students record all raw data, dates and changes to method in a logbook?
options: It replaces the need to analyse the data, because the raw values speak for themselves
It allows students to remove results later without anyone knowing they were there
It is required only for literature reviews, which rely on secondary data
It authenticates the work and gives a complete record of how the data were generated
questions.explanation: The logbook authenticates generated or collated data and documents every step, including modifications, so results can be checked. Removing data without a record would undermine authentication.

questions.stem: In a VCE Environmental Science scientific poster, what is the role of the communication statement in the centre of the poster?
options: A detailed description of each step in the method, in the order completed
A table of all the raw data collected over the whole investigation
A one-sentence summary of the key finding that answers the investigation question
A full list of all the references and acknowledgements used in the whole investigation
questions.explanation: The communication statement reports the key finding in one sentence and occupies the centre of the poster. Methods, data and references appear in their own sections.
